extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students, and readers studying experimental methods and the philosophy/methodology of physical science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on methods for investigating variations (collective, periodic, integrated), resonance, and the approximate character of scientific laws; intended to help design, interpret, and critique physical experiments and models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective Experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Herschel's 'Collective Instances' (adopted here as 'Collective Experiments'): experiments that exhibit at a glance the results of a general law by rendering visible undulations, patterns, or aggregate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such experiments often give the first hint of a law but may not admit exact measurement; they are most useful for popular illustration. Exceptions occur when the curves are precise and permanent (e.g., coloured figures from crystalline plates, Newton's rings, diffraction fringes), which may admit very accurate measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualizing motions of gases and liquids
rubrics_metrics.description: Render visible the motions of gas or liquid by diffusing some opaque or reactive substance in it so that flow, mixing, or currents become apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: strewing sand on vibrating plates; polarised light for crystalline plates; wax to show unequal heat conduction; smoke for air motions (smoke rings, jets); lycopodium powder for liquids; very dilute solutions (salt + silver nitrate) that produce a visible cloud where they meet. Use to reveal movements otherwise unapparent; choose a tracer appropriate to medium and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify periodic vs secular variations
rubrics_metrics.description: A periodic phenomenon is one which, with uniform change of the variable (time), returns repeatedly to the same value; a secular variation proceeds uniformly over long times without recurring phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurrence and repeatability to classify: pendulum swings, planetary revolutions are periodic; strictly rectilinear motion free from external forces is secular (hypothetical). Empirically regard non-recurrence as secular; note that many apparent secular trends may be periodic on very long timescales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate periodic variation from repeated arbitrary experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: An arbitrary series of raises and lowers or other controlled changes at will does not constitute a periodic variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such arbitrary repeated changes should be treated as a succession of distinct experiments that establish cause-and-effect, not as evidence of an underlying periodic law. Periodicity requires recurrence at (nearly) equal intervals independent of the experimenter's arbitrary schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurrence at equal intervals as evidence of connexion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a phenomenon recurs at equal or nearly equal intervals, the theory of probability gives considerable evidence of connexion between occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this probabilistic reasoning when matching periodicities (e.g., repeated comet appearances suggesting identity of the body; recurrence of tides matching moon's meridian passages). Recurrence together with similarity of other properties strengthens inference of causal relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of forced vibrations
rubrics_metrics.description: "If one part of any system... be continually maintained... in a state of regular periodic motion, that motion will be propagated throughout the whole system... and will give rise... to periodic movements executed in equal periods..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use matching periods across different parts of a system to infer propagation of a periodic cause. Examples: tides influenced by sun and moon, aberration of starlight attributed to Earth's annual motion, meteorological phenomena correlated with sun-spot cycles. Consider possible phase differences (not necessarily synchronous maxima/minima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangle superposed periodic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Many periodic causes may act together; by the superposition principle small periodic effects approximately add, producing complex resultant variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect compound behaviours (periods within periods). Ask iterative diagnostic questions: Is the periodic variation uniform? If not, is the change uniform? Is that change itself periodic? etc. Practical example: ocean tides composed of multiple constituents (semi-diurnal, diurnal, monthly, annual). Use decomposition methods to isolate components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for integrated (accumulated) effects and phase lag
rubrics_metrics.description: Some observed quantities are integrated effects of a driving periodic cause, so maxima/minima of effect lag behind maxima/minima of cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: air temperature peaks several hours after solar heating; hottest day typically about a month after the summer solstice; tidal effects lag the moon's direct attraction. When relating cause to effect, account for integration over time (mathematical integration) and resulting phase shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resonance and phase-dependent accumulation/cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated strokes or periodic inputs that are synchronous with a system's natural vibration accumulate energy (resonance); strokes in opposite phase cancel and dissipate energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize amplification when inputs reinforce (e.g., striking a pendulum at the same phase, musical resonance in strings and pipes, bridges failing under synchronized marching). Recognize cancellation when inputs are out of phase (e.g., neutralisation in clocks connected by wood-work). In analysis predict possibility of large long-period effects from small periodic forcings (planetary resonances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize approximate character of experimental knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental investigation yields approximate knowledge; we must distinguish between what can be known and what cannot, and avoid asserting absolute exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even successful mathematical descriptions (e.g., Kepler's laws) are approximations when applied to real bodies. Proving exact forms would require impossible precision. Always be explicit about the degree of approximation and avoid overclaiming exact truth beyond observational reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute simple/hypothetical models with awareness of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians/physicists replace complex real objects by idealized ones (straight lines, triangles, perfect fluids, homogeneous spheres) to render problems tractable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such idealizations when discrepancies are small enough not to alter the character of the solution, but remain conscious that all conclusions are conditional on these hypotheses. Verify applicability and estimate the effect of neglected complexities where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect negligible quantities only when justifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations often proceed by neglecting quantities unlikely to produce effects appreciable in observation; these rejections make the problem approximate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify omissions on the grounds of observability and estimated magnitude. Example: astronomers neglect perturbations from distant systems when effects are imperceptible. Beware that neglected small terms may accumulate (see resonance/integration) or become relevant with improved measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for instrumental and methodological limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: All measuring instruments and theoretical assumptions are imperfect; errors and idealizations limit the conclusions attainable from observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: plumb-line deviates due to local mass; mercury surfaces deviate from perfect plane; pendulum isochronism only holds for very small arcs; torsion balance assumes linear torsion for small angles. Quantify instrument/systematic errors and incorporate them into interpretation; treat perfect instruments and perfectly rigid/ideal bodies as useful fictions, not realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer practical robustness over theoretical perfection where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A theoretically superior method may be practically inferior; methods that are robust and yield truer results in practice can be preferred over theoretically ideal methods that are impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the common pendulum (not strictly isochronous) can be better in practice than the cycloidal pendulum (isochronous in theory but mechanically difficult); spherical surfaces easier and sufficiently accurate for many optical uses though not theoretically optimal. Balance theoretical accuracy against mechanical feasibility, noise, and instrument imperfections.
